question: What delivery guarantee should the system promise?
options: A) Best-effort at-least-once: in-memory queue, bounded retries, storage removes duplicates by event_id; documented loss cases (queue full, crash, retries exhausted, Close timeout) | B) Best-effort at-most-once: no retries (bugsnag-go model); no duplicates but more loss on transient failures and deploys | C) Durable delivery: client disk spool or message broker; much more complex and excluded by the proposal unless required
v1_bugsnag_parity: B - at-most-once like bugsnag-go: no retries; a failed send is logged and dropped. Changes proposal sections 3.1 and 5 (bounded retries) until retries are added later.
why_long_term: Retries recover from short outages and service restarts; duplicates are removed by event_id so the cost is small. C adds infrastructure the proposal excludes unless the business requires it.
how_bugsnag_handles_it: bugsnag-go is best-effort at-most-once: no retries, any non-200 response or network error is only logged, and queued events are lost on crash. Exception: unrecovered panics are reported by the default panic handler (panicwrap) from a watching parent process. Bugsnag's mobile SDKs persist and retry; the Go SDK does not.
bugsnag_source: bugsnag-go v2/report_publisher.go; bugsnag-go v2/payload.go; bugsnag-go v2/configuration.go

question: When should the service return success for a batch?
options: A) After validation only | B) After queuing in an in-memory server buffer that writes to storage asynchronously | C) After the processor/storage call returns successfully (synchronous)
v1_bugsnag_parity: Not covered: Bugsnag's server is a hosted black box. Suggest C (acknowledge after the processor returns): simplest and stateless.
why_long_term: The SDK already batches, so a server buffer adds a second loss window and a second queue to tune. C keeps the service stateless, makes graceful shutdown lossless and gives natural backpressure. Cost: RPC latency includes the storage write; revisit if the chosen database needs large buffered inserts.
how_bugsnag_handles_it: bugsnag-go treats any HTTP 200 as delivered and never learns what happens afterwards. Bugsnag's server-side processing after the 200 is not documented in the sources checked.

question: If a batch contains some invalid events, what should the service do?
options: A) Accept the valid events and return per-event rejections (event_id + reason) with status OK; rejected events are never retried | B) Reject the whole batch as INVALID_ARGUMENT (client drops all of it) | C) Reject the whole batch as retryable (risks endless retry loops)
v1_bugsnag_parity: bugsnag-go sends one event per request and the v1 SDK will send one event per RPC, but the contract keeps an events list and per-event results (Bugsnag's own payload also has an events array) so batching can be added later without a new contract.
why_long_term: One bad event should not cost hundreds of good ones, and because rejections are not retried there are no loops.
how_bugsnag_handles_it: Not directly comparable: bugsnag-go sends one event per HTTP request, so success or failure is all-or-nothing for that event. The payload format has an events array, but there are no per-event results.

question: Who generates event IDs, and how are duplicates from retries handled?
options: A) SDK generates a UUIDv7 when the event is captured; the same ID is sent on every retry; storage removes duplicates on (project, event_id) | B) Same as A but UUIDv4 (random, not time-ordered) | C) Server generates IDs; duplicates cannot be detected, so retries may store an event twice
v1_bugsnag_parity: Bugsnag sends no event ID. Suggest the SDK still sets event_id (no retries or dedup in v1) so retries can be added later without a contract change.
why_long_term: Stable IDs are what make retries safe. UUIDv7 is time-ordered, which keeps database indexes compact. Scoping by project stops one client from claiming another client's IDs.
how_bugsnag_handles_it: The bugsnag-go payload has no event ID; Bugsnag assigns IDs on the server and does not deduplicate. bugsnag-go avoids duplicates simply by never retrying.

question: Where should per-process fields (service, environment, app version, hostname, SDK version) be sent?
options: A) Once per batch in a source block; the server copies them into every stored event | B) Repeated on every event, exactly as in the proposal's section 4 table
v1_bugsnag_parity: Bugsnag repeats app/device data on every event. With one event per RPC both options cost the same; suggest A so later batching needs no contract change.
why_long_term: Smaller payloads and a single place to check against the API key. Stored events still contain every section 4 field, so the data model does not change.
how_bugsnag_handles_it: Bugsnag repeats app (version, releaseStage, type) and device (hostname, OS, runtime) blocks inside every event; this costs little because bugsnag-go sends one event per request. The API key and notifier info are sent once per request.

question: What value types may custom attributes (Fields) hold?
options: A) Flat map; each value is a string, int64, double or bool | B) Flat map of strings only (SDK converts every value to text) | C) Nested JSON-like values (google.protobuf.Struct)
v1_bugsnag_parity: Bugsnag allows nested values in tabs (tab -> key -> any value); the proposal's API uses flat Fields. Pick A (flat scalars, proposal shape) or C (nested, Bugsnag shape).
v1_status: ANSWER NEEDED - parity differs from proposal
why_long_term: Keeps types for later filtering while staying easy to size-limit and validate. Changing this later breaks the contract. Nested values are hard to bound and query.
how_bugsnag_handles_it: MetaData is tabs of key -> any value. Nested maps, slices and structs are converted at send time (structs via reflection, exported fields only). No size, depth or string-length limits are applied by the client.

question: How should stack traces be captured and represented?
options: A) Structured frames {function, file, line}, captured where Error() is called, capped (64 frames) | B) Same as A, but first reuse a stack already attached to the error through a Callers() []uintptr method (no extra dependency) | C) Same as B, plus pkg/errors StackTrace() support (adds github.com/pkg/errors to every service) | D) One preformatted string
v1_bugsnag_parity: C - like Bugsnag: call-site stack (max 50 frames), but reuse a stack already on the error (Callers(), pkg/errors StackTrace()). bugsnag-go already depends on pkg/errors, so services using Bugsnag have it today.
why_long_term: Structured frames can be size-limited and used for grouping later. Reusing an attached stack shows where an error started rather than where it was reported, at the cost of a few lines and no dependency. C pulls a dependency into every service.
how_bugsnag_handles_it: Captures the call-site stack with runtime.Callers (max 50 frames), but first reuses a stack already on the error (Callers() []uintptr, pkg/errors StackTrace(), StackFrames()). Frames are structured {method, file, lineNumber, inProject}; ProjectPackages (default main*) marks in-project frames.
bugsnag_source: bugsnag-go v2/errors/error.go; bugsnag-go v2/event.go; bugsnag-go v2/configuration.go

question: What should error_type contain when an error is wrapped (fmt.Errorf with %w, errors.Join)?
options: A) Type of the innermost error in the Unwrap() chain (first error for errors.Join); message keeps the full err.Error() text | B) Type of the outermost error (often *fmt.wrapError, which says nothing) | C) Outermost type plus the whole cause chain sent as a list (type, message, stack per level)
v1_bugsnag_parity: C - like Bugsnag: error_type is the outermost type, and every error in the Unwrap() chain is sent as a cause with its own type, message and stack.
why_long_term: The innermost type is the useful one, and Bugsnag also groups on the innermost error. C sends more data per event; it can be added later as a new field without breaking the contract.
how_bugsnag_handles_it: errorClass is the Go type of the error passed in (outermost, e.g. *fmt.wrapError). Each error in the Unwrap() chain is sent as an extra exception with its own class, message and stack, and grouping uses the innermost one. Since v2.6.4 callers can override the class and message explicitly.

question: Which severity levels should exist?
options: A) INFO, WARNING, ERROR (plus UNSPECIFIED = 0, always rejected) | B) A plus DEBUG | C) A plus FATAL/PANIC as its own level
v1_bugsnag_parity: A, plus Bugsnag's separate 'unhandled' flag for panics. Error() reports at ERROR as the proposal shows (Bugsnag's Notify defaults to warning).
why_long_term: Matches the proposal. If the panic helper (B7) is approved, add a separate 'unhandled' flag like Bugsnag instead of a new level.
how_bugsnag_handles_it: error, warning, info. Notify() defaults to warning (handled). AutoNotify panics are error and marked unhandled; Recover() panics are warning and handled. 'Unhandled' is a separate flag, not a severity.

question: Which fields should be added to the event model?
options: A) app_version (fixes the gap between sections 3.1 and 4), received_at (set by server), project (set by server from the API key), hostname | B) Same as A without hostname | C) Only app_version | D) Custom list (write it in your_notes)
v1_bugsnag_parity: A plus OS/runtime version and SDK name/version, like Bugsnag's app and device blocks. Bugsnag also sends user (id, name, email), context and HTTP request data; these are not in the proposal and stay out unless you say otherwise.
why_long_term: app_version is already required by section 3.1; received_at and project are trusted server values; hostname helps find the failing instance. None of them are tracing fields.
how_bugsnag_handles_it: Sends app.version, app.releaseStage, app.type, device.hostname (defaults to os.Hostname), OS and runtime versions, and notifier name/version. The project comes from the API key and event IDs are assigned by the server.

question: What happens when an event is bigger than the limits?
options: A) SDK truncates oversized fields at UTF-8 character boundaries and sets a truncated flag; server rejects anything over its hard limits | B) SDK sends as-is; server truncates | C) SDK drops oversized events entirely
v1_bugsnag_parity: Like Bugsnag: no client-side truncation; the server rejects events over a hard limit (about 1 MB, as Bugsnag) and the event is lost. One required difference: the SDK replaces invalid UTF-8, because JSON silently does this for Bugsnag but protobuf refuses to encode the event.
v1_status: DECIDED - parity (+ UTF-8 fix required by gRPC)
why_long_term: Keeps the event instead of losing it, the server never silently changes data, and one huge event can no longer fail a whole batch.
how_bugsnag_handles_it: bugsnag-go does no client-side truncation. The server enforces a payload limit (about 1 MB according to third-party copies of the API spec and a bugsnag-php issue; whether it answers 400 or 413 is unclear), and the whole event is lost.

question: How should events dropped inside applications become visible to operators?
options: A) SDK Stats() counters, plus drop counters sent in each batch header and exposed as server metrics per service | B) SDK Stats() only (every application must export them itself) | C) Log messages only
v1_bugsnag_parity: Bugsnag only logs drops; proposal section 5 asks for a dropped-event metric. Suggest log plus a simple Stats() counter (small); pure parity would be log only.
why_long_term: Operators see client-side loss in one place without wiring metrics into every app; counts arrive with the next successful batch.
how_bugsnag_handles_it: Drops are only written to the Logger ('Events channel full. Discarding value'); the caller is not told and there are no counters.

question: Accept these provisional limits until load testing replaces them in Phase 6?
options: A) Accept: queue 10,000 events / 16 MiB; batch 500 events / 1 MiB; flush every 1 s; RPC deadline 5 s; 3 retries with 200 ms to 5 s backoff and jitter; message 8 KiB; 64 attributes; 64 stack frames; server receive limit 4 MiB | B) Accept with changes (write them in your_notes)
v1_bugsnag_parity: Parity values: queue 100 events, 50 stack frames, one event per RPC, no retries, server limit about 1 MB per event. Bugsnag sets no request timeout, but over gRPC a hung call would block the single sender forever and proposal 3.1 requires RPC timeouts, so keep a 5 s deadline.
why_long_term: Values only need to be reasonable for development and tests; Phase 6 replaces them with measured ones.
how_bugsnag_handles_it: Queue of 100 events, 50 stack frames, one event per request, no retries, no HTTP timeout by default (depends on the configured Transport), server payload limit about 1 MB.

question: How should SDK clients authenticate to the service?
options: A) API key sent as bearer metadata over TLS; stored as a SHA-256 hash; can only submit events; several active keys per scope for rotation | B) mTLS / service identity (needs an existing service mesh or PKI, see B1b) | C) API key now, switch to mTLS later if a mesh is adopted
v1_bugsnag_parity: A - like Bugsnag: one API key per project, sent with every request over TLS, submit-only.
why_long_term: Simplest option that meets section 3.2 and works anywhere. Authentication lives in one interceptor, so mTLS can replace it later without touching the contract.
how_bugsnag_handles_it: One notifier API key per project, sent in a request header over HTTPS. It can only submit events; reading data needs a separate Data Access token. Regenerating a key invalidates the old one immediately, so there is no overlap window for rotation.

topic: API key scope and meaning of 'project'
question: What does one API key allow, and what is a 'project'?
options: A) Key -> project; the project lists allowed services (optionally environments); a batch naming any other service is refused | B) One key per service; the service is taken from the key and the payload value is ignored | C) Key -> project only; service and environment are free text from the client
v1_bugsnag_parity: C - like Bugsnag: key -> project; service and environment are set by the client. Meets proposal section 6 ('service or project').
why_long_term: A team can share one key across its services while a key still cannot write as an unrelated service (section 6). B is stricter but means more keys to manage. C does not meet section 6.
how_bugsnag_handles_it: Key -> project (usually one application). Release stage and app type are free text set by the client; there is no per-service restriction inside a project.

question: How should the SDK queue be bounded, and what is dropped when it is full?
options: A) Bounded by event count and bytes; drop newest; info/warning admitted only while the queue is below about 80% full, errors up to 100% | B) Count and bytes; drop newest; no severity priority | C) Count only; drop newest (bugsnag-go model) | D) Drop oldest instead of newest
v1_bugsnag_parity: C - like bugsnag-go: count-bounded queue (default 100, configurable as proposal 5 requires), drop newest when full and log it; no byte bound, no severity priority.
why_long_term: Logs and errors share one queue; without priority a burst of info logs pushes out the errors this project exists for. A byte bound caps memory.
how_bugsnag_handles_it: Buffered channel of 100 events drained by one goroutine (since v2.5.0; earlier versions started a goroutine per event). Sending never blocks; when full the newest event is discarded and logged. No byte limit, no severity priority.

question: How should the SDK retry failed sends?
options: A) SDK's own loop: retry UNAVAILABLE, DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, ABORTED, INTERNAL, UNKNOWN, and RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED only when the server sends RetryInfo; exponential backoff with full jitter; same event IDs; one batch in flight | B) gRPC built-in retry policy (service config) | C) No retries (bugsnag-go model)
v1_bugsnag_parity: C - no retries, like bugsnag-go. Changes proposal sections 3.1 and 5 for v1.
why_long_term: Built-in retries are invisible to drop counters, limited by gRPC's retry buffer, and cannot tell rate limiting from an oversized message. C loses events on every transient failure or deploy.
how_bugsnag_handles_it: No retries. Any non-200 response or network error is logged and the event is dropped.

question: What should the public SDK API look like?
options: A) Client type created with New(Config) (*Client, error); package-level Init/Info/Warn/Error delegate to a default client; Flush(ctx) and Close(ctx); EnabledEnvironments list and a disabled mode; Error(nil) is a counted no-op | B) Global-only API as in the proposal example (Init + package functions) | C) Client type only, no package-level functions
v1_bugsnag_parity: Bugsnag: global Configure + Notify(err, ...); no Flush/Close; cancelling MainContext drains the queue with no deadline. Proposal 3.1 and 5 require Flush and Close with bounded timeouts, and Info/Warn with plain messages (Notify needs an error). Suggest the proposal's Init/Info/Warn/Error + Flush(ctx)/Close(ctx), with Bugsnag-style AutoNotify/Recover; pure parity would drop Flush/Close.
v1_status: ANSWER NEEDED - parity conflicts with proposal
why_long_term: Keeps the Bugsnag-like one-liners from the proposal while tests and libraries can use their own instance. Context-based Flush/Close gives bounded shutdown.
how_bugsnag_handles_it: Global Configure plus Notify(err, rawData...) where rawData is a variadic list (severity, MetaData, User, Context, context.Context, *http.Request). bugsnag.New creates extra notifiers. No Flush/Close: if MainContext is set, cancelling it drains the queue synchronously with no deadline. Notify(nil) logs an error and sends nothing. EnabledReleaseStages limits which environments send.

question: Should the SDK help report panics? (Not in the proposal - addition.)
options: A) Recover() helper for defer: reports synchronously with a short timeout, marks the event unhandled, then re-panics | B) A plus net/http middleware that uses it | C) Process-level crash capture like Bugsnag's panicwrap (program re-runs itself as a child process) | D) No panic support
v1_bugsnag_parity: C + B - like Bugsnag: Init starts a panicwrap monitor process (github.com/bugsnag/panicwrap, MIT) that reports crashing panics synchronously; plus AutoNotify (report + re-panic), Recover (report + swallow) and net/http middleware, because net/http recovers handler panics itself so they never reach the monitor. Caveats: code before Init runs twice; app stderr flows through the monitor; Linux/macOS only.
why_long_term: Crashes are the most valuable errors and are exactly what an in-memory queue loses. A small explicit helper covers it; C changes how the process starts, which is invasive for a library. B is easy to add later.
how_bugsnag_handles_it: Default PanicHandler uses panicwrap: the program re-executes itself as a child and the parent reports panics (including fatal runtime errors and stack overflows) from the child's output. Also AutoNotify (synchronous send, unhandled, re-panics), Recover (normal send, swallows the panic) and HTTP middleware.

options: A) Only events sent through SDK calls (Info/Warn/Error) | B) A plus existing log/slog calls through an adapter (see B8) | C) A plus existing stdout/file logs through a log shipper (new component, much larger scope)
v1_bugsnag_parity: A - like Bugsnag: only events sent through the SDK.
why_long_term: Keeps volume predictable and matches the proposal's SDK-based design.
how_bugsnag_handles_it: Not a log system: only events sent with Notify or captured panics.

question: Should errors be grouped by fingerprint in this phase?
options: A) Defer; structured stack frames keep it possible later without a breaking change | B) Compute a fingerprint on ingest now (error type + top in-project frame) | C) Let the SDK send a custom grouping key
v1_bugsnag_parity: A - defer. Bugsnag groups on its server for its dashboard, which is out of scope.
why_long_term: Grouping matters mostly for a UI, which is out of scope; adding a fingerprint field later does not break the contract.
how_bugsnag_handles_it: Groups on the server, by default by error class plus file and line of the top in-project frame of the innermost exception; SDKs can override with a custom GroupingHash.

question: How should services move off Bugsnag?

topic: Operational alerts for the reporting system

options: A) Client drop rate, rejection rate, authentication failures, processor errors, p99 ingest latency, service availability | B) A subset (list it in your_notes)
